batches.literal_commit_message: Add literal Śrīdhara renderings for ŚB 3.28.11–41

additions.text: He states the gateway-functions of prāṇāyāma and the other limbs with respect to samādhi. By prāṇāyāma one removes faults such as disorders of wind and phlegm. “Contacts” means contacts with sense objects. “The non-lordly” means attachment and the like. Dhāraṇā is making the mind steady together with the vital breath; dhyāna is the continuous stream of the steadied mental modification; samādhi is the cessation of that modification. This is their distinction.

“Well concentrated” means that the mind has become steady. “Kāṣṭhā” means a part or manifestation, that is, the form. One whose gaze is upon the tip of his own nose is so described. This is prescribed in order to ward off both torpor and distraction.

He describes Hari, the object of meditation, in seven verses. The construction “one should meditate on Him whose lotus face is gracious” is completed by the sixth of these verses. His two eyes are ruddy like the interior of a lotus, and He is dark like the petal of a blue lotus.
His two silk garments are yellow like the filaments of a shining lotus. The Śrīvatsa is the mark upon His chest. His neck is closely adorned by the resplendent Kaustubha jewel.
The garland is accompanied by the sweet humming of intoxicated bees. He is surrounded by it. His necklaces and other ornaments are exceedingly precious, beyond valuation.
His hips shine with the cord of His girdle. The lotus-hearts of the devotees themselves are His seat. He increases, that is, gladdens, the minds and eyes of the devotees.
His appearance to the devotees is exceedingly beautiful. He abides in the age of youth, at the threshold of adolescence. He is eager and intent upon bestowing grace upon His servants.

His fame is worthy of praise and itself a holy place. It brings renown to those celebrated in sacred verse, headed by Bali. All His limbs are complete and perfect. He does not fall away, depart, or wander from that form.
His activity, His līlā, is worthy of being beheld.

Having thus described meditation on the complete form, he now teaches meditation on each individual limb. One should take the mind that has obtained a firm footing in Him and mark it out, making it specifically fixed on one place—that is, on one limb at a time.

He describes that meditation in order from the feet upward in thirteen verses. One should contemplate thoroughly. On the soles of the feet are line-shaped marks such as the thunderbolt; thus the feet are richly marked. Their lofty, reddish, shining nails form a circle whose moonlight strikes away the darkness in the hearts of great meditators. All these qualifying features are stated precisely because they are to be meditated upon.

Moreover, from washing His feet issued the foremost river, the Gaṅgā. By bearing upon his head that sacred water which carries one across saṃsāra, even Śiva became truly auspicious—that is, he attained exceedingly great bliss. For the meditator, the Lord’s foot is like a thunderbolt hurled against the mountain of sin in the mind. Alternatively, it is the foot upon which the thunderbolt-shaped mark is impressed.

The two knees of the all-pervading Lord and the two shanks extending up to them are caressed and served with skillful touch by Lakṣmī, the mother of Brahmā, the creator of all. To prevent the false impression that the Lord is subject to saṃsāra, He is called “unborn.” One should place these limbs in the heart, that is, meditate upon them.

Upon the two shoulders of Suparṇa rest the Lord’s limbs that are repositories of strength. They shine with the radiance of an atasi flower. His yellow garment hangs down as far as the ankles, and His rounded hips are embraced by the band of His girdle. The earlier instruction “one should place in the heart” is to be supplied here as well.

One should meditate upon the navel-lake of Hari. It is situated in the belly that is the cave, the abode, of the aggregate of worlds. In that navel-lake arose the lotus that is the seat of Brahmā, the self-born, and that comprises all the worlds. One should also meditate upon His two breasts, like two excellent emerald gems, made fair and bright by the rays of His spotless necklaces.

One should place in the mind the chest, the dwelling of the great Lakṣmī of the supreme Lord, and also His neck. His neck is such that the Kaustubha jewel, worn for ornament, is itself more greatly ornamented by resting there—the neck adorns the Kaustubha rather than merely being adorned by it. Both chest and neck bring delight to the minds and eyes of those who remember Him.

His arms bear armlets and bracelets polished to brilliance, and the guardians of the worlds take shelter upon them. One should contemplate the discus with a thousand spokes, whose splendor cannot be endured, and the Lord’s lotus hand in which it rests like a royal swan upon a lotus.

One should remember the mace smeared with the mire that is the blood of enemy warriors, and upon His neck the garland and the jewel, resounding with the voices of a swarm of bees. The jewel represents the principle of the individual living being. Thus the Viṣṇu Purāṇa says that Bhagavān Hari bears, in the form of the Kaustubha jewel, the self of this world, stainless, without guṇas, and untouched.

He has assumed this form through the compassion conceived toward His servants. His spotless cheeks are illuminated by the movement of His flashing makara-shaped earrings, and His nose is noble and prominent.

One should meditate on that face which, by its own beauty, surpasses the lotus attended by bees and serving as the abode of a pair of fish and of Śrī. His curls surpass the bees, and His two eyes surpass the pair of fish; in another comparison, His eyes themselves are like lotuses. His brows shine forth, and the whole form manifests within the mind.
The glance cast from His eyes is exceedingly full of compassion. It is joined with a gentle, affectionate smile and contains abundant grace. One should behold it in the cave of the heart.

One should meditate on Hari’s smile, which dries up the ocean of tears produced by the intense sorrow of all the worlds bowed before Him, and on His exceedingly noble circle of brows. By His own māyā those brows are fashioned to bewilder even the bearer of the fish-banner, Kāma. This is for the sake of the sages: the very god of desire who approaches to bewilder the sages is himself bewildered.

Having described meditation on the gentle smile, he now teaches meditation on the open laugh. One should meditate on Viṣṇu’s broad laughter. Because of its extraordinary beauty it becomes an object of meditation without effort. Its beauty is this: a row of fine teeth, like jasmine buds, shines reddened by the abundant radiance of the lower lip. The devotee, established in the cavity of the body—the heart—and softened by the rasa of love, should set the mind upon that alone and should not desire to see anything separate from it; that is, he should not let the mind wander.

In two verses he describes samādhi. Yoga is of two kinds, seedless and with seed. In seedless yoga, even when practiced by the method taught in the Gītā—restraining the restless, unstable mind wherever it wanders and bringing it under control in the self—samādhi is difficult. With seed it is easy. When Hari, the embodiment of supreme bliss, is meditated upon, cessation of the mind arises of itself without effort. This was also stated earlier: devotion takes away the minds and vital breaths of those absorbed in Me and, even without their willing it, directs them to My subtle goal. Therefore this very yoga was introduced by the words, “I shall describe the characteristic of yoga with seed.” He now shows its effortless accomplishment. Through the path of meditation one obtains love for Hari; the heart melts through devotion, horripilation rises from joy, and one is repeatedly moistened by tears born of longing and submerged in the flood of bliss. Then one even releases the mind which had served, like a fishhook, as the means of grasping the otherwise hard-to-grasp Lord; one’s effort to hold the object of meditation becomes relaxed.

When the mind thus becomes without external objects in Bhagavān, it is consequently freed from dependence upon a separate support. Without relation to an object of meditation, it cannot continue as a distinct meditator; nor does sound or any other object arise as before, since through the experience of supreme bliss it has become detached from them. Therefore it reaches nirvāṇa, dissolution: abandoning the form of a mental modification, it is transformed into the form of Brahman, just as a flame, when its particular fuel is removed, is transformed into the general form of elemental fire. In this state one sees the one indivisible self without interval, free from division into meditator and meditated object. The reason is that the stream of guṇas—the limiting adjunct of body and the rest—has withdrawn.

Nor does he again enter saṃsāra like one who rises from sleep. That very Puruṣa is established in that greatness, the form of Brahman, and has reached final repose through the last cessation of the mind, which is devoid of ignorance; this distinguishes the state from deep sleep, where ignorance remains, whereas here it does not. The reason is that this state has been produced by the discipline of yoga. An objection is raised: if pleasure and pain are qualities of the self, how can unity with Brahman occur? He replies that the causality and experiencership of pleasure and pain that had previously been attributed to the self are assigned instead to the unreal agent, ego, produced by ignorance. One sees them as established in that ego alone, having directly realized the truth of the Supreme Self.

He has understood the true nature of jīva and Brahman. In two verses the text describes his liberation while living. The perfected person of the kind just described does not even take notice of the body—how much less pleasure and pain—whether the body has risen from its seat and remains there, has moved away from that place, or has returned there again under the force of destiny. This is because he has attained his own true nature; alternatively, it is that very body from which he has discerned his true nature. The illustration for failure to attend even to something present is a man blinded by intoxication, who does not notice whether the garment wrapped about his waist remains there or has fallen away.

Thus he is one for whom reality has awakened. The word “also” in “the body also” should be noted. Hence he experiences only the portion of karma that has already begun, without fixation upon it. The same is taught by the statement, “What delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who beholds unity?” If so, how can the body act or cease acting, or remain alive? He answers that the body too, moving under daiva—that is, a previous saṃskāra—continues to live, together with the vital breaths and senses, for as long as the karma that initiated it remains. Would renewed attachment not then arise? No. He does not again adopt that body, together with its world of sons and the rest, with the notions “I” and “mine”; he regards it like a dream body. He is one whose yoga has risen to and reached samādhi and for whom the reality, the truth of the self, has awakened.

In six verses he explains the manner of this awakening, beginning with “just as.” Even from a son or another person who, through excessive affection, has been regarded as one’s very self, the mortal person such as a father is distinct. Likewise Puruṣa is the seer of the body and the rest and is distinct from them.

Even where there is no separate spatial location, he states the difference by an illustration. Fire is distinct from a presently burning firebrand of wood, even though it arises from its own source and even though the wood may be regarded as fire itself. Those of extremely undiscriminating understanding even identify smoke as fire; nevertheless fire, which burns and illuminates the firebrand and existed before that particular burning state, is distinct from it. Likewise the seer of the elements and the rest is distinct from them; distinct even from that entity called jīva is what is called Brahman; and distinct also from pradhāna is Bhagavān, who sets it in motion. This is the meaning.
